name: Drug Repurposing
title: Drug Repurposing
answer: Drug repurposing is the search for new therapeutic uses for compounds that already have some safety or manufacturing history. In the field of drug discovery and molecular simulation, it sits alongside target identification and de novo design, but it starts from existing molecules rather than new ones. The work draws on molecular structures, gene expression signatures, electronic health records, and literature. It is part of The AI Physician because a repurposed drug can move toward patients faster than a novel compound, though it still needs clinical evidence.

sections.body: Drug repurposing is the search for new therapeutic uses for compounds that already have some safety or manufacturing history. In the field of drug discovery and molecular simulation, it sits alongside target identification and de novo design, but it starts from existing molecules rather than new ones. The work draws on molecular structures, gene expression signatures, electronic health records, and literature. It is part of The AI Physician because a repurposed drug can move toward patients faster than a novel compound, though it still needs clinical evidence.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for AI-driven repurposing includes large chemical and biological databases such as ChEMBL, PubChem, and DrugBank, plus omics repositories and clinical data warehouses. Computation runs on GPU clusters or cloud instances, often with knowledge graphs that link drugs, targets, pathways, and diseases. The site tracks 798 scientific models, and many of those models are built for tasks like signature matching or molecular property prediction that repurposing pipelines reuse. Data engineering, identity resolution, and version control are as important as the models themselves.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A repurposing study often begins with a hypothesis generated by signature matching, where a drug's transcriptional effect is compared against a disease signature. Network-based methods propagate information across protein interaction or knowledge graphs, while matrix factorization and deep learning rank candidate drug-disease pairs. Molecular simulation and docking can then estimate whether a drug binds a new target, and cheminformatics filters remove implausible hits. The output is a ranked list, not a proven therapy, so experimental validation in cells or animal models follows.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in repurposing turn on data provenance, licensing, and patient privacy, because the inputs may include proprietary chemical structures or identifiable health records. Off-label use rules, patent positions, and regulatory pathways for new indications all shape what can be done with a promising candidate. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, and it also tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which show that liability questions around AI outputs are live. Provenance matters for reproducibility, so teams document data sources, model versions, and preprocessing steps.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward foundation models that learn from molecular sequences, structures, and clinical text in one system. Federated learning and privacy-preserving computation may let institutions share signals without moving patient data. Regulators are beginning to ask for evidence that AI-generated repurposing hypotheses are validated, not just plausible. The likely direction is tighter integration between simulation, real-world evidence, and prospective clinical trials.
